transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-03
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (AE, Redwood), Priya Nair (SE, Redwood), Carlos Vega (SE), Marcus Liu (CTO, BluePeak), Helen Park (ML Eng), David Chen (Security), Sofia Ramos (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Redwood walked through API equivalence for common OpenAI/Anthropic/Together calls, demoed Console and Optimize suggestions, and agreed next steps for a short performance/cost POC.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have a full table today, uh, i'll kick off with quick context, then priya will jump into the parity mapping and console walkthrough. Marcus, thanks for looping in security and ml eng.

[00:22] Marcus: yeah thanks, jordan. we're looking to trim inference spend and simplify integration — we currently use openai for chat and together for some local models, plus an anthropic experiment. main ask is: can we swap to one api without regression in quality and understand cost/latency impact.

[00:37] Jordan: totally. that's the goal — show you side-by-side endpoints and the small code changes needed, plus the console ops and optimize levers. priya?

[00:45] Priya: cool, i'll share screen — starting with the simple mapping table. common patterns we see: openai.ChatCompletion -> redwood.chat.create (or stream variants), openai.Completion -> redwood.text.generate, embeddings endpoints map to redwood.embeddings.create. note: function-calling semantics are similar but the param names differ a bit. sometimes transcription swapped param names in the copy.

[01:15] Helen: can you show an actual code diff? our codebase is fairly large and we prefer minimal changes.

[01:25] Priya: yep — example: openai python client
openai.ChatCompletion.create(model="gpt-4", messages=msgs)
becomes
redwood.chat.create(model="redwood/gpt4-compat", messages=msgs)
we also show a streaming client: openai's streaming chunk -> redwood.chat.stream where you can subscribe to partial events. the sdk keeps the same event hooks.

[01:58] Marcus: that model name — redwood/gpt4-compat — is that a shim or actual model? latency and tokenization differences are critical for us.

[02:10] Priya: good question. it's a catalog name we use for a model variant validated for compatibility. there are some differences in tokenization and stop-seq handling; in the parity doc we list how to adjust temperature, max_tokens and stop tokens. most customers need one or two tiny prompt tweaks, not a full retrain.

[02:36] David: from security: we need to know data residency and encryption. does hosted API persist logs? what about KMS/HSM integration and private deployment?

[02:48] Jordan: short answer: hosted default retention is configurable; we have redwood.private for VPC/on-prem or VPC peering; KMS integration is supported for dedicated/private; we'll share SOC2 and encryption docs — carlos will attach them.

[03:10] Carlos: yes i'll drop links to our security artifacts in the shared folder after call. we also support SAML/SSO and RBAC for console access.

[03:28] Priya: walking through the console: route configs, per-route model overrides, and rollout policies. here's an example route that falls back from a bigger model to a quantized variant if latency exceeds threshold. you can set percent-based canary and automatic rollback on quality regressions.

[03:58] Helen: how is quality regression detected? we have a small eval set we run on each commit.

[04:09] Priya: great — Redwood Optimize ties evals to alerting. you can upload a prompt/eval set and get quality diffs across model versions or quantization profiles; alerts trigger when metric delta exceeds a bound. it also suggests quantization and batching settings given your latency SLO.

[04:40] Marcus: batching — i want more detail. our peak qps is spikey and we care about 95th p99 latency. batching often kills p99.

[04:53] Priya: yes we surfaced that: continuous batching is workload-aware — small window when throughput allows, short-circuiting for single-token low-latency calls. Optimize will recommend batch sizes per route, and the runtime dynamically switches based on queue depth and SLOs.

[05:15] Helen: embeddings: we use openai embeddings for semantic search. are there numerics differences? dimensionality?

[05:25] Priya: embeddings map is in the spreadsheet — some models have 1536 dims, others 1024; we map vector dims and give migration steps: reindexing strategy, hybrid search recommendations, and how to run A/B with small sample. we also show how to run fast rerank using the Redwood reranking endpoint.

[05:48] Sofia: is there a built in cost estimate for a given traffic profile? we want to compare token cost across models.

[05:58] Jordan: yep console has token-level cost breakdowns and simulated cost projections given model mix and qps. Optimize also simulates cost after quantization changes and batching. we'll include a rough estimate in the parity sheet we send.

[06:20] Marcus: curious about Together — we run some experiments there for local fine-tuned variants. can Redwood host customer fine-tuned models?

[06:32] Priya: Redwood supports onboarding custom models — dedicated/private is common for that. we have an onboarding flow in the Console and an inference spec. we also provide optimized kernels and quantization pipelines; for private deployments we can work through an air-gapped ingest flow.

[06:50] David: on private deployment, what are networking requirements? vpc peering? static IPs? audit logs?

[06:59] Carlos: we support VPC peering, private link-like options depending on cloud, and static egress via NAT. audit logs can be exported to your SIEM; we support long term retention for enterprise tiers.

[07:20] Jordan: shifting to a short live demo — priya will show a migration example from openai chat code to redwood sdk and then flip to Console.

[07:30] Priya: demo — terminal open: here's a small microservice that calls openai.ChatCompletion. swap client import, update endpoint and model name, change one param: stop -> stop_tokens, and update streaming handler to accept redwood.event.delta. small patch, about 6 lines. i ran this beforehand against our compatibility model with the same prompts.

[08:05] Helen: did you see any output format drift for our controlled json responses? we use a json schema enforcement step.

[08:16] Priya: json outputs were stable; sometimes the model inserts spaces or slightly different tokenization around punctuation — we recommend adding a lightweight validation step that re-parses and applies minor normalization if you rely on exact byte-for-byte outputs.

[08:38] Marcus: latency numbers from your internal tests?

[08:43] Priya: in our bench for that prompt set, median was similar to openai for the same-sized model, p95 varied depending on load. for p99 we recommend dedicated capacity if you need tight SLOs. we'll provide the bench harness so you can reproduce.

[09:05] Jordan: also worth noting pricing differences: hosted usage-based vs reserved capacity for dedicated. if you expect sustained heavy inference, reserved can be 30-50% cheaper. we'll include both scenarios in the estimate.

[09:20] Sofia: ok let's get into what we need for the POC — Helen, any infra constraints?

[09:27] Helen: we can run bench from our staging cluster, allowlist redwood IPs, and provide a 1M token sample. we need to confirm SAML SSO for access.

[09:36] David: and security will need the questionnaire filled and proof of SOC2 plus encryption at rest details.

[09:43] Jordan: understood. carlos will share docs and the questionnaire link.

[09:50] Priya: quick note on caching: prefix/KV cache can cut costs for repeated context; for retrieval-augmented workflows we often see big wins. it's pluggable and you can configure TTLs per route. some transcript noise: client said K V cache which is the same KV we're referencing.

[10:10] Marcus: any gotchas moving from Anthropic? we use their safety filters in some flows.

[10:18] Priya: safety tooling differs; Redwood offers content filters and can integrate with your existing safety pipeline. we'll include a mapping of Anthropic safety hooks to Redwood filtering options in the parity sheet.

[10:32] Jordan: i'll pause demo and open floor for questions.

[10:37] Helen: for embeddings reindexing, can you do incremental reindex? time to full reindex?

[10:44] Priya: incremental is supported — we recommend rolling reindex for large corpora, and we provide scripts to compare old vs new vectors and measure drift. time depends on corpus size — we'll provide rough throughput numbers in the POC plan.

[11:00] Marcus: what's the simplest low-risk migration path? maybe run Redwood for a subset of traffic, A/B against openai?

[11:10] Jordan: exactly — route-based canary: send 5-10% to Redwood, collect eval metrics and latency/cost, and then increase. Console supports traffic splitting and automatic rollback if evals fail.

[11:26] Sofia: what's the expected timeline for the bench POC? we want numbers in two weeks.

[11:32] Jordan: with materials from you by next Monday, we can run bench and return results in ~10 business days — so yeah, two weeks is feasible.

[11:45] Marcus: ok i'm comfortable with that. can you include a simple cost comparison showing the same model family? that helps our finance folks.

[11:52] Jordan: will do.

[12:00] David: last security Q: do you allow customer-managed keys for hosted?

[12:06] Carlos: customer-managed KMS is available on Dedicated and Private; hosted has encrypted-at-rest with our keys, but we can discuss extensions per contract.

[12:20] Jordan: great — wrapping up. Recap of next steps is in the notes; we'll send the parity spreadsheet, SDK diffs, bench harness, security docs, and propose POC kickoff times. appreciate the time.

[12:40] Marcus: thanks everyone. good demo.

[12:48] Meeting end.
